title: Waterfall lace shawl
subtitle: Cascading chevron lace rows worked top down in fingering weight.
excerpt: Chevron lace rows angle downward from the spine to create a cascading waterfall effect across a crescent shawl. The repeat is a four-row pattern that is straightforward to memorise after the first few repeats.
sourceNotes: Chevron lace construction synthesised from traditional zigzag lace principles present in 19th-century Shetland and Irish crochet sources. Top-down crescent shaping is a modern adaptation. Original pattern by Homemade.

glossaryTerms.definition: A lace pattern where yarn-over decreases and chain arches are arranged in a diagonal or zigzag line, giving the impression of a V-shape or angular cascade.
The central column of increases running down the back of a top-down shawl, from which stitches grow outward in each row.
Double crochet two together: a decrease that joins two stitches into one by working partway through each and then pulling the yarn through all three loops at once.
Wetting the finished piece and pinning it to open the lace fully before drying.

crochet.finishedSizeText: Crescent shawl, 155 cm wingspan x 50 cm deep at centre back, blocked.

content.text: A waterfall lace shawl is a crescent worked top down from the back neck edge. A central

of double increases grows the width as you go; chevron lace rows angle outward from it to create a cascading diagonal effect. The finished shawl is 155 cm across and 50 cm deep at centre back, blocked.
decreases to shift the columns of holes diagonally. After two pattern repeats (eight rows) the diagonal rhythm becomes easy to follow without counting every stitch.

items.name: Fingering weight yarn
items.substitutions: A wool or wool-silk fingering weight blocks well and holds the chevron angles sharply.

content.text: 16 dc (UK) x 10 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering weight with a 3.5 mm hook, blocked. The chevron lace fabric tends to be looser than plain double crochet; use a tighter tension gauge swatch in the actual pattern stitch if your yarn relaxes significantly.
Ch 5. Work (1 tr, ch 2, 1 tr) into the 5th ch from hook (one corner made). Turn. Row 1 (increase row): Ch 4 (counts as 1 tr, ch 1). 1 tr into same base stitch. Ch 2. (1 tr, ch 2, 1 tr) into the ch-2
space. Ch 2. (1 tr, ch 1, 1 tr) into the last tr. Turn. You now have 3 sections either side of the centre spine.

Row A (right side): Ch 3, 1 tr into first ch-1 space. *Ch 2, skip, dc2tog over next 2 sts, ch 2, 1 tr into next space*. Work across to spine, work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into spine space (spine increase). Work back to match the other side. Turn.
Row B (wrong side): Ch 3, 1 tr into ch-1 space. *Ch 2, 1 dc into ch-2 space, ch 2, 1 tr into next tr*. Repeat to spine, work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into spine. Mirror to end. Turn.
Row C (right side): Ch 3, *ch 2, dc2tog, ch 2, 1 tr*. Repeat to spine, increase at spine. Mirror. Turn.
Row D (wrong side): As Row B. Turn.
Repeat rows A-D until the shawl is 50 cm deep from the neck edge when held flat and unblocked. Work a plain treble border row, then fasten off.

Soak the shawl, press out water in a towel, then pin. Pin the two tip ends of the crescent first to the wingspan markers at 155 cm apart on the blocking mats, then pin the centre back point downward to 50 cm. Fill in with pins along each curved edge every 5 cm. Leave until fully dry.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: Waterfall shawls have a few common tension and shaping errors.

items.symptom: Chevron diagonals not aligning between rows
items.fix: Mark the dc2tog positions on Row A with stitch markers and check they shift one stitch to the right on Row C. The diagonal angle comes from this one-stitch shift.

items.cause: Too many increases at the spine
items.fix: The spine increase is always (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr), not more. Count the spine stitches after each row and confirm the total stitch count grows by 4 per full repeat.
Work the ch-3 turning chain loosely. If the edge still pulls, add a ch-4 turning chain and count it as the first treble plus one chain space.
